promptText: A team has added content-moderation guardrails to an AI feature. Why is that not equivalent to having completed the 'ethics review' for the system?
options: Guardrails are per-request, runtime checks against known, enumerable categories of bad output, while disparate impact and corpus bias are aggregate, structural failures visible only across many decisions -- a system can pass every guardrail check and still systematically disadvantage one group
Guardrails and ethics reviews check the exact same things, so completing one always completes the other
Ethics reviews are only required for systems that do not use any guardrails at all
Guardrails are strictly a legal requirement, while ethics reviews are a purely optional courtesy step
explanation: A guardrail examines the shape of one output at a time; disparate impact is a pattern across thousands of outputs, often invisible unless someone deliberately slices outcomes by a protected attribute -- exactly the kind of failure no per-request filter is positioned to catch.

promptText: What does the 'four-fifths rule' actually measure and flag?
options: It flags for investigation when the ratio of the lowest group's selection rate to the highest group's selection rate falls below 0.80, serving as a screening threshold rather than proof of bias or fairness
It requires that exactly 80% of all applicants from any group must be approved, regardless of qualification
It measures the percentage of guardrail rules that successfully blocked harmful output
It is a legal requirement that model accuracy must exceed 80% before deployment
explanation: The four-fifths rule divides the lowest-selected group's rate by the highest-selected group's rate; a ratio below 0.80 flags the pattern for investigation, but it doesn't by itself prove the cause is bias versus a genuine underlying difference.

promptText: Why is 'the model decided X' often not a defensible explanation to give a regulator or an affected customer?
options: A model's output emerges from a probability distribution over billions of parameters with no single legible internal reason, and its own stated reasoning may be a plausible-sounding rationalization rather than the true causal chain, similar to the hallucination risk
Regulators are legally prohibited from ever accepting any statement generated by software
It is actually a perfectly defensible and sufficient explanation in all cases
The phrase is too short; adding more words to the same explanation would make it fully defensible
explanation: Since a model's self-explanation isn't guaranteed to reflect its actual computation, what is actually achievable and defensible is procedural transparency -- documented model/prompt version, grounding data, and evaluation results -- not the model's own account of its reasoning.

promptText: What core problem does RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) address in a pretrained base language model?
options: A base model pretrained purely on next-token prediction has no built-in preference between helpful and harmful completions, so RLHF injects a human preference signal after pretraining to turn a raw text predictor into an assistant-like system
RLHF exists solely to reduce the number of parameters in a model to speed up inference
RLHF replaces the need for any tokenizer by training the model directly on raw audio waveforms
RLHF is used exclusively to increase a model's maximum context window length
explanation: Next-token prediction alone gives the model no preference between a toxic and a helpful completion; RLHF trains a reward model on human preference rankings and then fine-tunes the base model to produce outputs that reward model scores highly.

promptText: A team removes a protected attribute like race entirely from a model's input schema and concludes the model is now free of racial bias. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: This is 'fairness through unawareness' -- other correlated fields like zip code, name, or school attended frequently act as proxies that let the model reconstruct the excluded attribute's signal anyway
There is no flaw; removing a protected attribute from the schema always fully eliminates any related bias
The flaw is that removing the attribute makes the model illegal to deploy in every jurisdiction
The flaw is that removing an input field always reduces the model's overall accuracy on every task
explanation: Correlated proxy variables can carry much of the excluded attribute's predictive signal, so an audit must check outcomes by the excluded attribute directly rather than assuming its absence from the schema is sufficient.

promptText: Why should human-in-the-loop review for consequential AI decisions (medical, financial, legal) be scaled to the stakes of the decision rather than to the model's stated confidence?
options: Model confidence and model correctness are not the same thing, so a highly confident wrong answer is not a lower-priority case for review -- it may be a higher-priority one, since confident wrongness is exactly what a human is least likely to catch on their own
Confidence scores are never available from any production LLM, so stakes are the only usable signal
Regulations universally prohibit using confidence scores for any purpose in AI systems
High-confidence outputs are always correct, so reserving review for low-confidence outputs is strictly more efficient
explanation: A confidently wrong answer in a high-stakes domain is especially dangerous because a downstream human reviewer is less likely to question it -- so review routing should be driven by the domain's stakes, not by how confident the model claims to be.

promptText: In the COMPAS recidivism-scoring controversy, ProPublica and the vendor Northpointe both published mathematically correct but seemingly contradictory analyses. What does the underlying impossibility result explain about this?
options: When the true base rate of the outcome differs between groups, a single scoring system cannot simultaneously satisfy equalized odds (which ProPublica measured) and predictive parity/calibration (which Northpointe measured), except by coincidence
One of the two analyses must have contained a computational error, since both cannot be correct about the same system
The impossibility result shows that fairness metrics are meaningless and should never be computed
The result only applies to criminal justice systems and has no bearing on any other domain like lending or hiring
explanation: Kleinberg/Mullainathan/Raghavan and Chouldechova proved that when group base rates genuinely differ, equalized odds and predictive parity cannot both hold at once -- so both critiques could be simultaneously correct and simultaneously unsatisfiable together.

promptText: How does Constitutional AI differ from plain RLHF in terms of where the model's notion of 'good' behavior comes from?
options: RLHF's notion of good is implicit and scattered across many individual annotator judgments, while Constitutional AI trains against an explicit, written set of principles that a team can inspect, debate, and revise as a document
Constitutional AI eliminates the need for any human involvement at any stage of training, unlike RLHF
RLHF and Constitutional AI are two names for the identical training algorithm with no meaningful difference
Constitutional AI only works on audio models, while RLHF only works on text models
explanation: Constitutional AI relocates the 'whose values' question to an inspectable written document rather than leaving it as an emergent, undocumented property of a distributed annotator pool's aggregate preferences.

promptText: How does 'equalized odds' differ from 'equal opportunity' as a fairness metric?
options: Equal opportunity only requires the true positive rate to match across groups; equalized odds additionally requires the false positive rate to match, so a system could satisfy equal opportunity while still incorrectly approving unqualified people from one group far more often than another
Equal opportunity and equalized odds are identical formulas that always produce the same result
Equalized odds only applies to binary classifiers, while equal opportunity only applies to regression models
Equal opportunity requires matching false positive rates, while equalized odds requires matching only overall accuracy
explanation: Equal opportunity checks only that qualified people are correctly identified at similar rates across groups; equalized odds is stricter, additionally requiring the false-alarm (false positive) rate to also match across groups.

promptText: What is a 'dual-use' AI capability, and why does it complicate a model release decision differently than an ordinary bug?
options: It is a capability with clearly legitimate beneficial applications and a plausible path to serious harm using the exact same underlying function, so the mitigation must involve controlling access or context rather than removing the capability, which would also remove its legitimate value
It refers to any model that can process both text and images in the same request
It refers to a model that has been fine-tuned by two separate organizations for two different purposes
It is a capability that only becomes harmful after the model has been deployed for more than one year
explanation: A dual-use capability's harm depends entirely on the user's intent, not a flaw in the capability itself, so you cannot simply patch it away without also destroying its legitimate, beneficial use.

promptText: Why is staged/phased release of a new AI model or capability described as analogous to a canary deployment in ordinary software engineering?
options: Both limit blast radius by exposing a risky change to a small group first, observing real-world usage to surface unanticipated failures before scaling exposure further, rather than releasing to everyone simultaneously
Both techniques exclusively apply to reducing infrastructure hosting costs, with no connection to safety
Canary deployments and staged AI releases are legally required to use identical traffic percentages by regulation
Staged release means the model is released only during a specific canary migration season each year
explanation: Just as a canary deployment routes a small percentage of traffic to a new version before ramping up, staged AI release exposes a model to a small group first, observing real-world failure modes at contained scale before wider exposure.

promptText: Why might a fairness or harm-review pipeline built on an LLM-judge be especially vulnerable to the same category of attack described for RAG evaluation judges?
options: If content flowing into the review pipeline is attacker-influenced (such as a user-editable knowledge base entry), the same prompt-injection risk that threatens an LLM-judge's faithfulness score can be aimed at a bias or harm-severity judge, attempting to manipulate it into scoring a harmful pattern as benign
LLM-judges are immune to prompt injection because they only see aggregated statistics, never raw content
This risk applies only to guardrail-layer filters, never to fairness or harm-review pipelines
Fairness review pipelines never use LLM judges, so this attack vector does not apply to them
explanation: A bias or harm-severity judge reasoning over potentially attacker-crafted content inherits the same manipulation risk as any LLM-as-judge evaluation -- adversarial content could be designed specifically to make a genuinely harmful pattern score as acceptable.

promptText: A staff engineer is deciding which fairness metric (demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalized odds, or predictive parity) to gate a lending-decision feature on. Why does the chapter insist this cannot be delegated as a purely technical implementation detail?
options: Because the impossibility result guarantees these metrics trade off against each other whenever group base rates genuinely differ, the choice is inherently a product and ethics decision about which kind of error to distribute unevenly, and must be made explicitly, documented, and revisited -- not defaulted to whichever metric a library computes first
Because only one of the four metrics is mathematically valid, and the others are provably incorrect formulas that should never be used
Because fairness metrics are purely aesthetic preferences with no real mathematical relationship to each other
Because regulators mandate that every AI system must use demographic parity exclusively, with no exceptions
explanation: Since the choice of fairness metric determines which tradeoff is accepted (and the impossibility result guarantees a tradeoff exists whenever base rates differ across groups), an undocumented default is itself an unaccountable ethical choice -- it belongs in a review gate with explicit sign-off, not left as an implementation detail.

promptText: What is the distinction between 'outer alignment' and 'inner alignment,' and why is inner misalignment harder to detect?
options: Outer alignment asks whether the specified training objective actually captures what you want; inner alignment asks whether the trained model actually internalizes that objective rather than a different proxy goal that merely correlates with good training performance -- inner misalignment is harder to detect because the model can pass every test on the training distribution while pursuing something subtly different underneath
Outer alignment refers to a model's behavior in production, while inner alignment refers only to behavior during training, with no other difference
Inner alignment is simply a synonym for outer alignment used by a different research group
Outer alignment is always easier to fix than inner alignment because outer misalignment cannot be detected by any evaluation method
explanation: Outer alignment failures stem from a poorly specified objective and are fixed by improving the specification; inner alignment failures are subtler because the model can perform well on every evaluation you run while actually optimizing for a different internal goal, revealed only by distribution shift or an uncovered edge case.

promptText: A team argues 'we can't control the base model's pretraining data, so bias isn't really something our application team is responsible for.' Why does this chapter reject that reasoning as an excuse?
options: Pretraining data is only one of several bias entry points; RAG corpus composition, fine-tuning/RLHF data, evaluation-panel diversity, and the production feedback loop are all fully within the application team's control and are each independently capable of producing a documented disparity, just like the base model itself
The reasoning is actually correct and fully absolves application teams of any responsibility for bias once a third-party model is used
Bias can only ever enter through pretraining data, so any other explanation for a disparity must be a measurement error
Application teams are only responsible for latency and cost, never for any aspect of model behavior or fairness
explanation: The chapter's bias-entry-point table names RAG corpus composition, fine-tuning data, evaluator bias, and the deployment feedback loop as entry points fully within an application team's control, regardless of what the foundation-model provider did during pretraining -- so 'we don't control the base model' is true but not an excuse.
